title: Humanistic Buddhism
hook: in Taiwan, movements bringing Buddhism into daily life, schools and hospitals

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hospice room, Angulimala's road and the practice of staying. Your line: in hard places.

A monastery with a university next door. A temple with a clinic on the ground floor, a library, a cafeteria serving vegetarian lunch to office workers, a weekend class for children. On a Taiwanese hillside or in a city building, some Buddhist movements look less like a retreat from the world and more like a small town built around kindness. That's on purpose. Their teachers say the Buddha's teaching belongs right in the middle of ordinary human life.
screen: `A TEMPLE WITH A CLINIC.` → `A SMALL TOWN OF KINDNESS.` → `ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: First, the name. In Chinese it's renjian fojiao, Buddhism in the human world. Its teachers say it isn't a new school, just a way of putting the weight back where they believe it belongs: on the living, on this life, not mainly on funerals or heavens far away. Second, the teachers behind it. In modern China, a monk named Taixu called for Buddhism to turn toward the living, to educate monks and nuns and to serve society. His student Yin Shun took that thread further, and Buddhist teachers who came to Taiwan carried it with them. Third, the text they lean on. Humanistic teachers point out that the Buddha was born, woke up and taught as a human being, among people. And they return to the old teaching that a human birth is hard to come by. The Dhammapada puts it in a short verse which, simply put, runs: hard to win is a human life, hard to come by is hearing the teaching. If this life is that precious, they say, don't save your practice for later. Fourth, what it looks like. In Taiwan, large movements grew around teachers such as Master Hsing Yun of Fo Guang Shan and Master Sheng Yen of Dharma Drum Mountain. They built schools, universities and temples abroad, and taught that a kind word at work, an honest day's labor and a patient hour with your kids are all practice. Tomorrow, another movement, built around relief. Not every Buddhist puts the weight the same way; some value retreat and renunciation more, and humanistic teachers would say those have their place too. But this movement's question is simple: if you have a human life today, what will you do with it?
screen: `BUDDHISM IN THE HUMAN WORLD.` · `TAIXU AND YIN SHUN.` · `A HUMAN BIRTH IS RARE.` · `SCHOOLS, HOSPITALS, WORKPLACES.` · then, large: `THIS HUMAN LIFE.`

segments.voice: Let the room you work in come to you, a desk, a counter, a classroom, a kitchen at home, and the people in it, one at a time, until one face stays. Breathe in, noticing that they too have a human life, rare and brief. Breathe out, and let one small, real kindness for them come to mind.
Humanistic Buddhism. Buddhism in the human world: practice brought into daily life, schools, hospitals and work, because this human life is the place to practice. Today's word.
Your line: this human life. Rare, brief, and already here in your hands. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Humanistic Buddhist movements, especially in Taiwan, run temples alongside schools, universities, hospitals and social services, and teach lay members to treat their work and family life as practice.

chat.says: Why does that Buddhist temple run a clinic and schools? Aren't temples just for prayer?
options: Humanistic Buddhists say practice belongs in this human life, so serving others counts.
It pays for the temple, since donations alone can't keep the monks fed and housed.
It's a government rule in Taiwan that every temple must run a public service.
chat.meaning: Renjian fojiao, Buddhism in the human world, puts the weight on the living and this life, so schools, clinics and work become places of practice.
